newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends higher in U.S. after news of Deng's death.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends higher in U.S. after news of Deng's death.

text.p: The dollar rose against most major currencies Wednesday, hitting its session highs on news China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping had died, traders said.
Investors bought dollars, traditionally a safe-haven in times of political turmoil, as rumors began to swirl in the currency market that the sickly, 93-year-old Deng had died.
The dollar spiked to a high of 1.7005 marks, but quickly fell back to its prior level before China's Xinhua news agency stamped the rumors official.
Xinhua reported Deng died late Wednesday of complications from Parkinson's disease and a lung infection.
Meanwhile, the dollar steadily inched higher against the yen, closing near its session high of 124.57 yen.

"They were buying dollars and dollar/mark popped up past a resistance level at 1.70 marks, but it has come off since," said Doug Lee, assistant vice president at Sakura Bank Ltd in New York, adding the market had widely anticipated the news.
The dollar rose to 124.50/60 yen at the close from 123.95/00 yen at the open and to 1.6975/85 marks from 1.6915/25 marks.
Earlier, the dollar climbed higher due to the heavy buying of dollars by large, speculative money funds.
Some dealers expressed surprise over the dollar's sharp reversal of fortune on Wednesday following its steep slide on Tuesday against most major currencies.

"I am a little surprised. People did liquidate yesterday, selling dollars and buying marks and yen, but it seems like everything has reversed right back," said Ben Strauss, an associate vice president at Bank Julius Baer and Co.
The dollar suffered a minor set back in early U.S. trade after the Commerce Department released surprisingly strong U.S. international trade data for December.
The U.S. trade gap widened 29.6 percent to $10.29 billion from a revised $7.94 billion in November.

Simultaneously, the dollar was also hit by a Labor Department report showing consumer prices remained well-behaved in January. The Consumer Price Index rose a tame 0.1 percent in January, less than the 0.3 percent increase expected by Wall Street economists.
Neither set of data was seen as supportive of the dollar, with soft inflation figures taking the pressure off the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates and the trade gap growing more than expected.
Dealers said the figures were not shocking enough to erase positive dollar sentiment. The U.S. currency remained largely unfazed by conflicting statements from Geman central bank officials overnight.

The Bundesbank's February monthly report and remarks from its chief Hans Tietmeyer weighed on the dollar in European trade. The report said the mark's rally since early 1995 had more than corrected. Also, the German mass-circulation Bild newspaper quoted Tietmeyer as saying he hoped the dollar's long-term rise against the mark was at an end.

However, a subsequent media report quoted Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke as saying a dollar level between 1.70 to 1.75 marks would not risk importing inflation into Germany and boosted the dollar.

In other trading, sterling rose to $1.6158/68 from $1.6145/55 at Wednesday's open. The dollar rose to Canadian $1.3597/02 from C$1.3547/52 and to 1.4853/60 Swiss francs from 1.4777/82. The Australian dollar rose to $0.7675/80 from $0.7646/51.
